paragraphs: Principal Causes Which Tend to Maintain the Democratic Republic in the United States

A democratic republic exists in the United States, and the main purpose of this book has been to explain why it exists. As my subject carried me along, I passed over several of the causes that help sustain the institutions of America, or only hinted at them. Others I have been unable to discuss. And those I have dwelt on most are, so to speak, buried in the details of the earlier parts of this work. So before I go on to speak of the future, I think the best thing I can do is to gather into a small space the reasons that best explain the present. In this chapter I look back, and I shall be brief. I shall only remind the reader, in the briefest way, of what he already knows, and I shall select only the most prominent of the facts I have not yet pointed out.
All the causes that help maintain the democratic republic in the United States can be reduced to three heads:—
I. The unusual and accidental situation in which Providence has placed the Americans.
III. The manners and customs of the people.

Accidental or Providential Causes Which Contribute to the Maintenance of the Democratic Republic in the United States The Union has no neighbors — No metropolis — The Americans have had the chances of birth in their favor — America an empty country — How this circumstance contributes powerfully to the maintenance of the democratic republic in America — How the American wilds are peopled — Avidity of the Anglo-Americans in taking possession of the solitudes of the New World — Influence of physical prosperity upon the political opinions of the Americans.

A thousand circumstances, independent of human will, combine to make it easier to maintain a democratic republic in the United States. Some of these peculiarities are well known, and the others can easily be pointed out. But I shall limit myself to the most prominent among them.

The Americans have no neighbors, and so they have no great wars, financial crises, invasions, or conquests to fear. They need neither heavy taxes nor large armies nor great generals. And they have nothing to fear from a scourge more dangerous to republics than all these evils together: military glory. It is impossible to deny the immense influence that military glory has on the spirit of a nation. General Jackson, whom the Americans have twice elected to head their government, has a violent temper and mediocre talents. Nothing in the whole course of his career ever showed that he is qualified to govern a free people, and indeed the majority of the educated classes of the Union has always opposed him. Yet he was raised to the Presidency, and has been kept in that high position, solely by the memory of a victory he won twenty years ago under the walls of New Orleans. That victory, however, was a very ordinary achievement, and it could only be remembered in a country where battles are rare. And the people that is carried away in this manner by the illusions of glory is unquestionably the coldest and most calculating, the least military (if I may use the expression), and the most prosaic of all the peoples on earth.

America has no great capital city *a whose influence is felt, directly or indirectly, over the whole country. I consider this one of the chief causes of the maintenance of republican institutions in the United States. In cities it is impossible to prevent people from acting in concert and stirring one another into sudden and passionate resolutions. Cities may be regarded as large assemblies in which every inhabitant is a member. Their populace has an enormous influence on the magistrates, and often carries out its own wishes without their involvement.

a [ The United States has no metropolis, but it already contains several very large cities. In 1830 Philadelphia counted 161,000 inhabitants and New York 202,000. The lower classes who live in these cities form a rabble even more dangerous than the populace of European towns. They consist, first, of freed Black people, whom the laws and public opinion condemn to a hereditary state of misery and degradation. They also include a multitude of Europeans who have been driven to the shores of the New World by misfortune or misconduct. These men infect the United States with all our vices, and they bring with them none of the interests that might counteract their harmful influence. Because they live in a country where they have no civil rights, they are ready to turn every passion that stirs the community to their own advantage. Thus, within the last few months, serious riots have broken out in Philadelphia and in New York. Disturbances of this kind are unknown in the rest of the country, which is not at all alarmed by them, because the city population has so far had no power or influence over the rural districts. Nevertheless, I regard the size of certain American cities, and especially the nature of their population, as a real danger to the future security of the democratic republics of the New World. I venture to predict that they will perish from this cause, unless the government manages to create an armed force that will stay under the control of the national majority while remaining independent of the city population and able to put down its excesses.

[The population of the city of New York had risen, by 1870, to 942,292, and that of Philadelphia to 674,022. Brooklyn, which may be said to form part of New York City, has a population of 396,099 in addition to that of New York. The frequent disturbances in the great cities of America, and the excessive corruption of their local governments, over which there is no effective control, are among the greatest evils and dangers of the country.]]

To subject the provinces to the metropolis is therefore to do two things. It places the fate of the empire in the hands of one part of the community, which can be condemned as unjust. It also places it in the hands of a populace acting on its own impulses, which must be avoided as dangerous. The dominance of capital cities is therefore a serious blow to the representative system. It exposes modern republics to the same defect as the republics of antiquity, which all perished because they did not know that form of government.

I could easily list a great number of secondary causes that have helped establish the democratic republic of the United States and that help maintain it. But among these favorable elements I discern two principal ones, which I hasten to point out. I have already observed that the origin of the American settlements can be seen as the first and most effective cause to which the present prosperity of the United States may be attributed. The Americans had the chances of birth in their favor. Their forefathers brought with them into the country that equality of conditions from which the democratic republic has very naturally grown. Nor was this all they did. Besides this republican state of society, the early settlers handed down to their descendants the customs, mores, and opinions that contribute most to the success of a republican form of government. When I reflect on the consequences of this first circumstance, I seem to see the destiny of America contained in the first Puritan who landed on those shores, just as the whole human race was represented by the first man.

The chief circumstance that has favored the establishment and the maintenance of a democratic republic in the United States is the nature of the territory the Americans inhabit. Their ancestors gave them the love of equality and of freedom, but God himself gave them the means of remaining equal and free, by placing them on a boundless continent open to their efforts. General prosperity favors the stability of all governments, but especially of a democratic constitution. A democracy depends on the dispositions of the majority, and above all on that part of the community that is most exposed to the pressure of want. When the people rules, it must be made happy, or it will overturn the State. And misery can drive it to the same excesses to which ambition drives kings. The physical causes, independent of the laws, that help promote general prosperity are more numerous in America than they have ever been in any other country in the world, at any other time in history. In the United States, not only is the legislation democratic, but nature herself favors the cause of the people.

In what part of human tradition can we find anything similar to what is happening before our eyes in North America? The famous communities of antiquity were all founded among hostile nations, which they had to subjugate before they could flourish in their place. Even the moderns have found, in some parts of South America, vast regions inhabited by a people of inferior civilization, who nevertheless occupied and cultivated the soil. To found their new states, the settlers had to wipe out or subdue a numerous population, until civilization was made to blush for its success. But North America was inhabited only by wandering tribes, who gave no thought to the natural riches of the soil. That vast country was still, properly speaking, an empty continent, a desert land awaiting its inhabitants.

Everything is extraordinary in America, the social condition of the inhabitants as well as the laws. But the soil on which these institutions are founded is more extraordinary than all the rest. When the Creator first placed man on the earth, the earth was inexhaustible in its youth, but man was weak and ignorant. By the time he had learned to uncover the treasures it contained, hosts of his fellow creatures covered its surface, and he had to win a refuge of rest and freedom by the sword. At that very time North America was discovered, as if it had been kept in reserve by the Deity and had just risen from beneath the waters of the flood.

That continent still shows, as it did in the earliest times, rivers that rise from never-failing sources, green and moist solitudes, and fields that the farmer’s plow has never turned. In this state it is offered to man. It is offered not to man in the barbarous and isolated condition of the early ages, but to a being who already holds the most powerful secrets of the natural world, who is united with his fellow men, and who has been instructed by the experience of fifty centuries. At this very moment thirteen million civilized Europeans are peacefully spreading over those fertile plains, whose resources and extent they do not yet know accurately themselves. Three or four thousand soldiers drive the wandering Native American tribes before them. The pioneers follow the soldiers. They cut through the woods, scare off the beasts of prey, trace the courses of the inland streams, and prepare the triumphal march of civilization across the wilderness.

Others have so often described the favorable influence of America’s material prosperity on the institutions of that country, and I myself have so often mentioned it, that I shall not dwell on it beyond adding a few facts. People commonly hold a mistaken notion that the deserts of America are peopled by European emigrants who land every year on the coasts of the New World, while the American population grows and multiplies on the soil its forefathers tilled. In fact, the European settler usually arrives in the United States without friends, and sometimes without resources. To survive he has to work for hire, and he rarely goes beyond the belt of industrious population next to the ocean. The desert cannot be explored without capital or credit, and the body must be accustomed to the hardships of a new climate before it can be exposed to the risks of forest life. It is the Americans themselves who leave the places of their birth every day to acquire extensive lands in a remote country. Thus the European leaves his cottage for the shores across the Atlantic, and the American, who was born on that very coast, plunges in his turn into the wilds of Central America. This double emigration never stops. It begins in the remotest parts of Europe, it crosses the Atlantic Ocean, and it advances across the solitudes of the New World. Millions of men are marching at once toward the same horizon. Their language, their religion, and their customs differ, but their object is the same. The gifts of fortune are promised in the West, and to the West they turn their steps. *b

b [ [The number of foreign immigrants into the United States in the last fifty years (from 1820 to 1871) is stated to be 7,556,007. Of these, 4,104,553 spoke English—that is, they came from Great Britain, Ireland, or the British colonies; 2,643,069 came from Germany or northern Europe; and about half a million from the south of Europe.]]

Nothing can be compared with this continuous movement of the human race, except perhaps the invasions that preceded the fall of the Roman Empire. Then, as now, generations of men were driven forward in the same direction, to meet and struggle on the same ground. But the designs of Providence were not the same. Then, every newcomer was the herald of destruction and death. Now, every adventurer brings with him the elements of prosperity and life. The future still hides from us the further consequences of this westward migration of the Americans, but we can easily see its more immediate results. Every year a portion of the inhabitants leave the States where they were born. As a result, the population of those States grows very slowly, even though they were settled long ago. Thus in Connecticut, which has only fifty-nine inhabitants to the square mile, the population has not grown by more than one quarter in forty years, while that of England has grown by one third in the same period. The European emigrant therefore always lands in a country that is only half full, and where hands are in demand. He becomes a workman in comfortable circumstances. His son goes to seek his fortune in unsettled regions, and he becomes a rich landowner. The father accumulates the capital that the son invests, and neither the foreigner nor the native knows want.

The laws of the United States are extremely favorable to the division of property. But a cause more powerful than the laws prevents property from being divided to excess. *c This is easy to see in the States that are beginning to be thickly peopled. Massachusetts is the most populous part of the Union, yet it contains only eighty inhabitants to the square mile, which is much fewer than in France, where 162 are counted on the same area. But in Massachusetts estates are very rarely divided. The eldest son takes the land, and the others go to seek their fortune in the desert. The law has abolished the rights of primogeniture, but circumstances have combined to restore it in a form that no one can complain of, and that harms no just rights.
c [ In New England the estates are exceedingly small, but they are rarely subjected to further division.]

A single fact will be enough to show the enormous number of people who leave New England in this way to settle in the wilds. We were assured in 1830 that thirty-six members of Congress were born in the little State of Connecticut. The population of Connecticut, which makes up only one forty-third of that of the United States, thus supplied one eighth of the whole body of representatives. Yet the State of Connecticut itself sends only five delegates to Congress, and the thirty-one others sit for the new Western States. If these thirty-one men had remained in Connecticut, they would probably have remained humble laborers instead of becoming rich landowners. They would have lived in obscurity, unable to rise into public life. And far from becoming useful members of the legislature, they might have been unruly citizens.

These reflections do not escape the Americans any more than they escape us. “It cannot be doubted,” says Chancellor Kent in his “Treatise on American Law,” “that the division of landed estates must produce great evils when it is carried to such excess as that each parcel of land is insufficient to support a family; but these disadvantages have never been felt in the United States, and many generations must elapse before they can be felt. The extent of our inhabited territory, the abundance of adjacent land, and the continual stream of emigration flowing from the shores of the Atlantic towards the interior of the country, suffice as yet, and will long suffice, to prevent the parcelling out of estates.”

It is hard to describe the greed with which the American rushes forward to seize the immense prize that fortune holds out to him. In the chase he fearlessly faces the Native American’s arrow and the diseases of the forest. The silence of the woods does not impress him, and the approach of beasts of prey does not disturb him, for he is driven on by a passion more intense than the love of life. Before him lies a boundless continent, and he presses on as if time were short, and he were afraid of finding no room for his efforts. I have spoken of the emigration from the older States, but how shall I describe the emigration from the newer ones? Barely fifty years have passed since the State of Ohio was founded. Most of its inhabitants were not born within its borders. Its capital has been built only thirty years, and its territory is still covered by an immense stretch of uncultivated fields. Nevertheless the population of Ohio is already moving westward, and most of the settlers who go down into the fertile savannahs of Illinois are citizens of Ohio. These men left their first country to improve their condition, and they leave their new home to improve it still more. Fortune awaits them everywhere, but happiness they cannot reach. The desire for prosperity has become in their minds an ardent and restless passion that grows by what it gains. Early on, they broke the ties that bound them to their native soil, and they have formed no new ones along the way. Emigration was at first a necessity for them, a means of survival. It soon becomes a kind of game of chance, which they pursue as much for the excitement it brings as for the profit it yields.

Sometimes man’s progress is so rapid that the desert reappears behind him. The woods bend to make a passage for him, and spring up again when he has passed. In crossing the new States of the West, it is not unusual to come upon deserted dwellings in the middle of the wilds. The traveler often finds the remains of a log house in the most solitary retreats, and they bear witness to the power of man, and no less to his inconstancy. Over these abandoned fields and these ruins of a day, the primeval forest soon scatters fresh vegetation. The beasts return to the haunts that were once their own. And Nature covers the traces of man’s path with branches and flowers, which wipe out his fleeting track.

I remember that I was once crossing one of the wooded districts that still cover the State of New York, when I reached the shore of a lake set deep in forests as old as the world. A small island, covered with woods whose thick foliage hid its banks, rose from the middle of the water. On the shores of the lake nothing showed the presence of man, except a column of smoke on the horizon, rising from the treetops to the clouds. It seemed to hang from heaven rather than to climb toward the sky. A Native American boat had been hauled up on the sand, and it tempted me to visit the islet that had first caught my eye. In a few minutes I set foot on its banks. The whole island was one of those delightful solitudes of the New World that almost make civilized man regret the haunts of the savage. A luxuriant vegetation bore witness to the incomparable fruitfulness of the soil. The deep silence common to the wilds of North America was broken only by the hoarse cooing of the wood pigeon and the tapping of the woodpecker on the bark of the trees. I was far from supposing that this spot had ever been inhabited, so completely did Nature seem to have been left to her own whims. But when I reached the center of the island, I thought I discovered some traces of man. I then examined the surrounding objects with care, and I soon saw that a European had undoubtedly come to seek refuge in this retreat. Yet what changes had taken place in the scene of his labors! The logs he had hastily cut to build himself a shed had sprouted again. Even the props were intertwined with living greenery, and his cabin had become a bower. Among these shrubs a few stones could be seen, blackened with fire and sprinkled with thin ashes. Here the hearth had no doubt been, and the chimney, in falling, had covered it with rubble. For some time I stood in silent admiration of the exuberance of Nature and the littleness of man. And when I had to leave that enchanting solitude, I exclaimed sadly, “Are ruins, then, already here?”

In Europe we tend to regard a restless disposition, an unbounded desire for riches, and an excessive love of independence as tendencies very dangerous to society. Yet these are the very elements that ensure a long and peaceful life for the republics of America. Without these restless passions the population would gather in certain spots and would soon be subject to wants like those of the Old World, which are hard to satisfy. Such is the present good fortune of the New World that the vices of its inhabitants are scarcely less favorable to society than their virtues. These circumstances have a great influence on how human actions are judged in the two hemispheres. What we would call greed, the Americans often call praiseworthy industry. And they blame as faintheartedness what we regard as the virtue of moderate desires.

In France, simple tastes, orderly habits, domestic affections, and the attachment men feel to the place of their birth are regarded as great guarantees of the peace and happiness of the state. But in America nothing seems more harmful to society than these virtues. The French Canadians have faithfully preserved the traditions of their original customs, and they are already short of room on their small territory. This little community, which has only recently begun to exist, will soon fall prey to the calamities that afflict old nations. In Canada the most educated, patriotic, and humane inhabitants make extraordinary efforts to make the people dissatisfied with the simple enjoyments that still content them. There, the seductions of wealth are praised with as much zeal as the charms of an honest but limited income are praised in the Old World. More effort is spent there on exciting the passions of the citizens than elsewhere on calming them. If we listen to their praises, we shall hear that nothing is more admirable than to trade the pure and homely pleasures that even the poor man enjoys in his own country for the dull delights of prosperity under a foreign sky. We shall hear that it is admirable to leave the family hearth and the turf beneath which one’s forefathers sleep, in short, to abandon the living and the dead in search of fortune.

At present America offers a field for human effort far more extensive than any amount of labor that can be applied to work it. In America too much knowledge cannot be spread, for all knowledge, while it may serve the one who possesses it, also benefits those who do not. New wants are not to be feared, since they can be satisfied without difficulty. The growth of human passions need not be dreaded, since all passions can find an easy and legitimate object. Nor can men be given too much freedom, since they are scarcely ever tempted to misuse their liberties.

The American republics of today are like companies of adventurers formed to explore the wastelands of the New World together and to carry on a flourishing trade. The passions that stir the Americans most deeply are not political but commercial. Or, to put it more accurately, they bring the habits they form in business into their political life. They love order, without which business does not prosper, and they set a special value on regular conduct, which is the foundation of a solid business. They prefer the good sense that builds large fortunes to the enterprising spirit that so often squanders them. General ideas alarm their minds, which are used to positive calculations, and they hold practice in higher honor than theory.

It is in America that one learns to understand the influence that physical prosperity has on political actions, and even on opinions that ought to acknowledge no authority but reason. This truth is most visible among foreigners. Most of the European emigrants to the New World bring with them that wild love of independence and of change that our calamities so readily produce. I sometimes met Europeans in the United States who had been forced to leave their own country because of their political opinions. They all astonished me by what they said, but one of them surprised me more than all the rest. I was crossing one of the most remote districts of Pennsylvania when night overtook me, and I had to beg for hospitality at the gate of a wealthy planter, a Frenchman by birth. He asked me to sit down by his fire, and we began to talk with the freedom that suits people who meet in the backwoods, two thousand leagues from their native country. I knew that my host had been a great leveler and an ardent demagogue forty years earlier, and that his name was not unknown to fame. So I was more than a little surprised to hear him discuss the rights of property as an economist or a landowner might have done. He spoke of the necessary gradations that fortune establishes among men, of obedience to established laws, of the influence of good morals in commonwealths, and of the support that religious opinions give to order and to freedom. He even went so far as to quote an evangelical authority in support of one of his political tenets.

I listened, and I marveled at the weakness of human reason. A proposition is true or false, but amid the uncertainties of science and the conflicting lessons of experience, no art can prove it to be one or the other until some new event clears away the clouds of doubt. I was poor, and I become rich. I should not expect prosperity to act on my conduct and leave my judgment free. My opinions change with my fortune, and the happy circumstances I turn to my advantage supply the decisive argument that was missing before. The influence of prosperity acts even more freely on the American than on foreigners. The American has always seen public order and public prosperity, intimately united as they are, advance together before his eyes. He cannot conceive that one can exist without the other. He therefore has nothing to forget, and he has no need, like so many Europeans, to unlearn the lessons of his early education.
Influence of the Laws on the Maintenance of the Democratic Republic in the United States
Three principal causes of the maintenance of the democratic republic — Federal Constitutions — Municipal institutions — Judicial power.

The principal aim of this book has been to make the laws of the United States known. If this purpose has been accomplished, the reader is already able to judge for himself which laws really tend to maintain the democratic republic and which ones endanger its existence. If I have not succeeded in explaining this over the whole course of my work, I cannot hope to do so within the limits of a single chapter. I do not intend to retrace the path I have already followed, and a very few lines will be enough to sum up what I have already explained.
Three circumstances seem to me to contribute most powerfully to the maintenance of the democratic republic in the United States.
The first is the Federal system of government that the Americans have adopted. It allows the Union to have the power of a great empire together with the security of a small State.
The second consists in the municipal institutions that limit the despotism of the majority, and at the same time give the people a taste for freedom and a knowledge of the art of being free.

The third lies in how the judicial power is constituted. I have shown how the courts of justice help hold back the excesses of democracy, and how they restrain and steer the impulses of the majority without halting its activity.
Influence of Manners on the Maintenance of the Democratic Republic in the United States

I have remarked before that the manners of the people may be considered one of the general causes to which the maintenance of a democratic republic in the United States is due. Here I used the word manners in the sense the ancients gave to the word mores. I apply it not only to manners in the proper sense, that is, what makes up the character of social intercourse. I extend it to the various notions and opinions current among men, and to the mass of ideas that form their cast of mind. I therefore include under this term the whole moral and intellectual condition of a people. My intention is not to draw a picture of American manners. It is simply to point out those features of them that favor the maintenance of political institutions.
Religion Considered as a Political Institution, Which Powerfully Contributes to the Maintenance of the Democratic Republic Among the Americans

North America peopled by men who professed a democratic and republican Christianity—Arrival of the Catholics—Why the Catholics form the most democratic and the most republican class at the present time.

Every religion is found alongside a political opinion connected to it by affinity. If the human mind is left to follow its own bent, it will regulate the temporal and spiritual institutions of society on one uniform principle. Man will try, if I may use the expression, to bring the state in which he lives on earth into harmony with the state that he believes awaits him in heaven. Most of British America was peopled by men who had shaken off the authority of the Pope and acknowledged no other religious supremacy. They brought with them into the New World a form of Christianity that I cannot describe better than by calling it a democratic and republican religion. This sect contributed powerfully to the establishment of a democracy and a republic. From the earliest settlement of the emigrants, politics and religion formed an alliance that has never been dissolved.

About fifty years ago Ireland began to pour a Catholic population into the United States. On the other side, the Catholics of America made converts, and at present more than a million Christians professing the truths of the Church of Rome are to be found in the Union. *d The Catholics are faithful to the observances of their religion, and they are fervent and zealous in believing and defending its doctrines. Nevertheless they form the most republican and the most democratic class of citizens in the United States. This fact may surprise the observer at first, but on reflection the causes behind it are easy to discover.

d [ [It is difficult to ascertain accurately the size of the Roman Catholic population of the United States, but in 1868 an able writer in the “Edinburgh Review” (vol. cxxvii. p. 521) affirmed that the whole Catholic population of the United States was then about 4,000,000, divided into 43 dioceses, with 3,795 churches, under the care of 45 bishops and 2,317 clergymen. But this rapid increase is mainly supported by immigration from the Catholic countries of Europe.]]

I think people have been wrong to regard the Catholic religion as the natural enemy of democracy. Among the various Christian sects, Catholicism seems to me, on the contrary, to be one of the most favorable to the equality of conditions. The Catholic Church has only two elements in its religious community: the priest and the people. Only the priest stands above the rank of his flock, and everyone below him is equal.

On points of doctrine the Catholic faith places all human capacities on the same level. It subjects the wise and the ignorant, the man of genius and the common crowd, to the details of the same creed. It imposes the same observances on the rich and the poor, and inflicts the same austerities on the strong and the weak. It accepts no compromise with mortal man. It reduces the whole human race to the same standard, and it merges all the distinctions of society at the foot of the same altar, just as they are merged in the sight of God. Catholicism may dispose the faithful to obedience, but it certainly does not prepare them for inequality. The opposite may be said of Protestantism, which generally tends to make men independent more than to make them equal.

Catholicism is like an absolute monarchy. If the sovereign is removed, all the other classes of society are more equal than they are in republics. It has not infrequently happened that the Catholic priest has left the service of the altar to join the governing powers of society and take his place among the civil ranks of men. This religious influence has sometimes been used to secure the interests of the political order to which he belonged. At other times Catholics have taken the side of aristocracy out of a spirit of religion.

But as soon as the priesthood is entirely separated from the government, as it is in the United States, no class of men is found more naturally disposed than the Catholics to carry the doctrine of the equality of conditions into the political world. If, then, the Catholic citizens of the United States are not forcibly led by the nature of their beliefs to adopt democratic and republican principles, at least they are not necessarily opposed to them. And their social position, as well as their small numbers, obliges them to adopt these opinions. Most of the Catholics are poor, and they have no chance of taking part in the government unless it is open to all citizens. They are a minority, and all rights must be respected in order to secure them the free exercise of their own privileges. These two causes lead them, without their knowing it, to adopt political doctrines that they would perhaps support with less zeal if they were rich and dominant.

The Catholic clergy of the United States has never tried to resist this political tendency. Instead it works to justify what follows from it. The priests in America have divided the intellectual world into two parts. In one they place the doctrines of revealed religion, which command their assent. In the other they leave those truths that they believe have been freely left open to political inquiry. Thus the Catholics of the United States are at the same time the most faithful believers and the most zealous citizens.

It may be said that in the United States no religious doctrine shows the slightest hostility to democratic and republican institutions. The clergy of all the different sects speak the same language, their opinions agree with the laws, and the human intellect flows onward in one single current.

I happened to be staying in one of the largest towns in the Union when I was invited to attend a public meeting. It had been called to help the Poles and to send them supplies of arms and money. I found two or three thousand people gathered in a vast hall that had been prepared to receive them. After a short time a priest in his ecclesiastical robes stepped to the front of the platform. The spectators rose and stood with their heads uncovered while he spoke in the following terms:—
